text: Understanding how gene flow shapes contemporary population structure requires the explicit consideration of landscape composition and configuration. New landscape genetic approaches allow us to link such heterogeneity to gene flow within and among populations. However, the attribution of cause is difficult when landscape features are spatially correlated, or when genetic patterns reflect past events. We use spatial Bayesian clustering and landscape resistance analysis to identify the landscape features that influence gene flow across two regional populations of the eastern massasauga rattlesnake, Sistrurus c. catenatus. Based on spatially explicit simulations, we inferred how habitat distribution modulates gene flow and attempted to disentangle the effects of spatially confounded landscape features. We found genetic clustering across one regional landscape but not the other, and also local differences in the effect of landscape on gene flow. Beyond the effects of isolation-by-distance, water bodies appear to underlie genetic differentiation among individuals in one regional population. Significant effects of roads were additionally detected locally, but these effects are possibly confounded with the signal of water bodies. In contrast, we found no signal of isolation-by-distance or landscape effects on genetic structure in the other regional population. Our simulations imply that these local differences have arisen as a result of differences in population density or tendencies for juvenile rather than adult dispersal. Importantly, our simulations also demonstrate that the ability to detect the consequences of contemporary anthropogenic landscape features (e.g. roads) on gene flow may be compromised when long-standing natural features (e.g. water bodies) coexist on the landscape.

Keywords: anthropogenic disturbances, CDPOP, DNA microsatellites, landscape genetics, replicate landscapes, simulations Received 1 August 2012; revision received 15 May 2013; accepted 23 May 2013 Populations are genetically structured through the interplay of mutation, drift, selection and gene flow (Wright 1949, 1969; Slatkin 1987). Understanding how these forces interact across spatial and temporal scales is a dominant theme of evolutionary studies (Templeton 2006). Increasingly, however, we recognize that gene flow is modulated by physical and biotic heterogeneity in the environment. Quantifying the scale over which gene flow operates and thus the scale over which local adaptation or demographic independence might arise requires an approach that explicitly considers landscape variability. Landscape genetics encompasses this Correspondence: Stephen C. For example, identifying genetic disjunctions can illuminate the underlying ecological or historical processes promoting differentiation. However, genetic structure does not always result from an impermeable barrier. Instead, connectivity across a landscape might better reflect a series of features that interact through their relative contributions to overall spatial structure. Basic isolation-by-distance models (IBD; Wright 1943; Malecot 1955) fail to capture the heterogeneous nature of dispersal in complex landscapes, where topography influences gene flow (McRae 2006; Spear et al. 2010). A more realistic model accounts for the amenability to dispersal of the intervening landscape between individuals or populations and incorporates the effective distance between them rather than geographic distance alone. To calculate effective distances, researchers define a ‘resistance surface’ in a raster GIS environment, where each landscape feature is assigned a value reflecting the relative degree to which it supports or inhibits dispersal (Spear et al. 2010). Using Mantel (Mantel 1967) and partial Mantel (Smouse et al. 1986) matrix permutation tests, researchers can then evaluate hypotheses of how landscape affects dispersal by correlating genetic distance with distances derived from resistance surfaces (Spear et al. 2010). An issue in landscape genetics is unequivocal attribution of cause, complicated either because genetic signatures of particular features are spatially confounded, or because genetic patterns reflect past events not contemporary landscapes. Simulations show that partial Mantel tests used in a causal modelling framework can be a powerful tool for rejecting incorrect hypotheses of spatial structure (Cushman et al. 2006; Cushman & Landguth 2010; Shirk et al. 2010). Under this framework, competing models of spatial structure are created, each with exclusive predictions. Each model is subjected to a simple Mantel test against a matrix of genetic distances, and a set of partial Mantel tests factoring out the effect of the alterative models from the focal model, and vice versa. Although effective for discriminating among over-arching models of spatial structure (e.g. IBD vs. isolation by barrier vs. isolation by resistance, IBR), researchers are often more interested in selecting among competing hypotheses of IBR. In this case, model selection is commonly achieved by ranking Mantel correlation coefficients of significant IBR models (e.g. Schwartz et al. 2009; Quemere et al. 2010; Short Bull et al. 2011). With large risk of Type I error in landscape-level analyses (Balkenhol et al. 2009; Cushman & Landguth 2010; Guillot & Rousset 2013), an explicit evaluation of the accuracy of this approach is required. Of particular importance is assessing the ability of partial Mantel tests to reject incorrect hypotheses when landscape features with influences spanning different temporal scales are conflated in genetic models. For example, in some landscapes, artificial elements like roads often coincide with longstanding natural features such as valleys or water bodies. Thus, while contemporary genetic structure might appear to correlate with modern landscape features, in reality it reflects a legacy of historical habitat configuration. It is these contemporary landscapes that are of most interest to landscape geneticists, yet few studies consider the consequences of combining spatially confounded landscape elements in genetic models. Simulation modelling is well suited to disentangling historical vs. contemporary landscape effects on gene flow (e.g. Epps et al. 2005; Riley et al. 2006) and validating model choice (Cushman & Landguth 2010; Epperson et al. 2010; Shirk et al. 2012). For example, using partial Mantel tests, Vandergast et al. (2007) inferred that contemporary genetic structure of mahogany Jerusalem crickets (genus Stenopelmatus) correlated with a reconstructed historical landscape, but also with contemporary road fragmentation after controlling for landscape history. By simulating gene flow consecutively across the reconstructed and current landscapes, Vandergast et al. (2007) found that the observed genetic divergence in their empirical data set could have arisen during a contemporary time frame. Here, we combine landscape genetic analysis with individual-based simulations to test for the effects of spatially correlated landscape features on genetic structure of the eastern massasauga rattlesnake (Sistrurus c. catenatus): a thick-bodied, medium-sized (~55 cm) member of the Viperidae native to Southern Ontario and the north-central United States. Previous work suggested differentiation of populations across small (<5 km) spatial scales (Gibbs et al. 1997; Lougheed et al. 2000; Chiucchi & Gibbs 2010); however, it is unknown if landscape physiognomy contributes to this. Here, we identify the natural and anthropogenic landscape elements that might restrict gene flow. To determine the geographical consistency of genetic structure, we contrast the two largest remaining populations of the massasauga in Ontario, Canada: the shores of eastern Georgian Bay and the Bruce Peninsula. These regional populations share a common evolutionary history, with population divergence following postglacial recolonization (Ray et al. 2012). We also evaluate our ability to assess the effects of recent anthropogenic change on gene flow from those caused by long-standing landscape elements using simulations. Specifically we address the following:

How are massasauga populations structured, and what aspects of landscape might contribute to population break points? 2 What landscape features shape gene flow within diagnosed populations, and is this consistent between regions? 3 Can we distinguish between the genetic signatures of contemporary vs. historical factors that are spatially confounded using simulation methods?

Over three active seasons (May–October) from 2008 to 2010, we assembled 308 massasauga blood or tissue samples across two regional populations in Ontario, Canada: the northern Bruce Peninsula (n = 170) and the shores of eastern Georgian Bay (n = 138) (Fig. 1). For each sample, we recorded UTM coordinates of capture site with an accuracy of <10 m (see Appendix S1, Supporting Information for sampling details). Apart from extensive road networks, neither region has much anthropogenic disturbance, with tourism and recreation as the main land use category (Lawrence & Nelson 2005). The small town of Tobermory lies at the northern tip of the Bruce Peninsula. The town of Parry Sound (population 18 000) lies at the eastern terminus of Parry Sound (an extension of Georgian Bay) along the eastern Georgian Bay shoreline, dividing the study region into two approximately equally sized north and south sampling areas. Both regions have similar total area and density of roads that are bisected by at least one busy highway, and have extensive networks of secondary and tertiary roads (Fig. 1). The area south of Parry Sound in eastern Georgian Bay has a complex network of water bodies, and water surfaces account for 15% of the total landscape area compared to 9% north of Parry Sound and only 4% in the Bruce Peninsula. Massasaugas are more or less continuously distributed across both regional populations, and our sampling reflects this inasmuch as was possible. We also searched for road-killed snakes and obtained specimens from collaborators. We secured samples from two islands: Lyal Island (44° 56′ 48′′ N, 81° 24′ 16′′ W), which lies 2 km off the western shore of the Bruce Peninsula, and Beausoleil Island (44° 52′ 31′′ N, 79° 51′ 59′′ W; Georgian Bay Islands National Park), which lies <500 m from the southern mainland of eastern Georgian Bay.

We extracted DNA from blood and tissue using QIAGEN DNeasy Tissue kits (QIAGEN, Mississauga, ON, Canada) following the manufacturer’s protocol. We genotyped individuals at 12 microsatellite loci using seven published and five unpublished species-specific primers (see Appendix S1, Table S1, Supporting Information for details).

We tested for departures from Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) and for linkage disequilibrium using Arlequin (Excoffier & Lischer 2010) and Genepop (Raymond & Rousset 1995; Rousset 2008), respectively (see Appendix S1; Supporting Information for details). To determine the number of genetically distinct population clusters within eastern Georgian Bay, the Bruce Peninsula and globally, we used spatial Bayesian assignment implemented in the program TESS 2.3.1 (Chen et al. 2007). We first ran a global test using all samples to test whether the two regional populations are genetically distinct. Next, we ran TESS for the Bruce Peninsula and eastern Georgian Bay separately to determine the number of genetically distinct subpopulations within each region. For all tests, we ran 1 000 000 sweeps of MCMC following a burn-in of 500 000 sweeps using the BYM admixture model (Durand et al. 2009). We conducted 10 independent runs with kmax varying from 2 to 6. We chose the ideal cluster number based on when mean DIC values reached a plateau, or when bar plots of admixture coefficients stabilized. For each test, we did an additional 50 runs for the most likely value of kmax. We averaged the 10 runs with the highest likelihood using CLUMPP (Jakobsson & Rosenberg 2007) and visualized the resulting Q matrix in DISTRUCT (Rosenberg 2004).

We constructed a series of alternate hypotheses for our causal modelling framework, building from the de facto null model of IBD to a series of IBR where genetic distance between individuals is determined by the suitability of the intervening habitat matrix. Multiyear radio telemetry studies were previously conducted in both of our study regions, and we used these to define our landscape genetic models (Harvey & Weatherhead 2006; Rouse et al. 2011). Telemetry data showed that massasaugas are habitat generalists at the macrohabitat scale, using open habitat, wetlands and sparse forest in proportion to their availability, but tend to avoid dense forest during the active season (Harvey & Weatherhead 2006). Thus, we defined a ‘suitable’ land-cover category as a combination of open habitat (bedrock, alvar, abandoned fields), wetlands and sparse forest. We considered three land-cover types to be potential restrictors of massasauga movement: open water, dense forest and roads. Both open water and roads present significant dispersal barriers to many terrestrial snake species (King & Lawson 2001; Shine et al. 2004; Row et al. 2007, 2010; Clark et al. 2010), and we expect the same to be true for massasaugas, although they do successfully traverse roads and are capable of swimming across small water bodies (pers. We acknowledge that other features like gestation sites, hibernacula or topography may influence massasauga movement, but these are not included because (i) our considered landscapes are relatively flat, and (ii) we lack information on the location of either hibernacula or sites where females may gestate. We created multiple landscape resistance surfaces representing different combinations of these features using the Ontario Land-Cover Database, First Edition. In GRASS GIS 6.4 (GRASS Development Team 2010), we re-sampled raster maps to a 40-m resolution and reclassified them so that they included five cover types: open water, dense forest, major roads, minor roads and suitable. We quantified differences in landscape composition and configuration between regions using FRAGSTATS 3.3 (McGarigal et al. 2002; Appendix S1, Table S2, Supporting Information). The raster maps were cropped to include only the core massasauga range based on an updated range map for the species (Parks Canada 2010). Next, we assigned a categorical resistance value to each feature representing low, medium, high or very high resistance to dispersal. For this analysis, the relative resistance assigned is more important than the absolute value (Rayfield et al. 2010). Starting with an assignment of categorical resistances values from 1 to 4 (with 1 representing suitable landscape), we explored the effect of varying relative resistance of features within each model by applying a transformation from Shirk et al. We found that varying relative resistance did not change our overall inference of landscape effects on genetic structure, but that transforming values by a factor of 1.5 (giving categorical resistance of 1, 3, 5, 8) produced the strongest increase in Mantel correlation coefficients (Table S3, Supporting Information). Some combinations of landscape resistance values were not tested. For example, we hypothesized that dense forest would always present a lower resistance than open water to a dispersing massasauga, and thus this feature was only allowed to vary from low to medium resistance in any of the 18 IBR models. Table 1 details the 18 IBR models. We calculated pairwise resistance distance between individuals for each IBR model with CIRCUITSCAPE 3.5 (McRae & Beier 2007). This program combines circuit and random walk theories to measure connectivity between sampling locations. We chose this method over least-cost path because it averages resistance over all possible paths between pairwise samples, and we assume that juvenile snakes are na€ıve to the configuration of the surrounding environment and thus do not chose a single optimal path. To generate comparable distances, Circuitscape was used for the model of IBD as well by calculating pairwise resistance between indi- viduals across a neutral landscape (all cell values given a resistance of 1.0). As many of the IBR models included roads as a hypothesized restrictor of massasauga movement, we removed all road-killed samples from these analyses, reducing the sample size to 106 in eastern Georgian Bay (n = 29 north of Parry Sound, n = 77 south of Parry Sound) and 105 in the Bruce Peninsula. We used a causal modelling framework to rank the 18 alternative models of IBR and tested if any explained pairwise genetic distances within populations better than the null model of IBD (Cushman et al. 2006). First, we calculated the Mantel correlation between a matrix of interindividual genetic distances (ar; Rousset 2000) and matrices for each of the 18 IBR models, and the IBD model, using the ECODIST 1.2.3 package (Goslee & Urban 2007) in R (R Development Core Team 2011). Genetic distance matrices of interindividual Rousset’s ar (Rousset 2000) were generated using SPAGEDI 1.3 (Hardy & Vekemans 2002). Next, we tested for independent effects of each hypothesis by factoring out the effect of IBD from each IBR model and vice versa using partial Mantel tests. (2010); twostep causal modelling). For the top-ranked IBR model to be the only landscape hypothesis supported, a partial Mantel test with genetic distance controlling for each of the other IBR models must be significant, and the tests between the alternative IBR models with genetic distance controlling for the top IBR model must all be nonsignificant (Appendix S1, Supporting Information).

Anthropogenic landscape features present a unique problem in landscape genetics because they often are built in areas that are most amenable to construction. Indeed, our study regions are popular summertime destinations and roads often run alongside water bodies, and these two features are significantly spatially correlated (Table S7, Supporting Information). Thus, a possible confound exists where our analyses might imply that roads are barriers to gene flow when in fact, impediments result from other facets of topography. To disentangle the effects of water and roads, we performed individual-based and spatially explicit simulations of gene flow using the program CDPOP 1.0 (Landguth & Cushman 2010). Our objectives were twofold: first we quantified how many generations must pass before a road would be detectable as a barrier to gene flow to test whether genetic disjunctions could occur within time frames relevant to anthropogenic disturbance. Second, we investigated our ability to detect roads as barrier to gene flow when long-standing water barriers are also present on the landscape. For our first objective, we simulated gene flow across a hypothetic 500 km2 square landscape. For the first 100 generations, individuals dispersed and mated following IBD (neutral landscape). After 100 generations, a linear road assigned a resistance value of 3 was introduced onto the landscape to represent a semipermeable barrier and remained on the landscape for 50 further generations. Because juvenile natal dispersal distances are unknown for wild massasaugas and population size varies across regions, we ran simulations using three different juvenile dispersal thresholds (1.77, 2.00 or 2.20 resistance units) across two populations densities (low: 4/km2 or high: 6/ km2), producing six sets of simulations. Resistance units are not directly comparable to geographic distance, but preliminary runs showed that thresholds of 1.77, 2.00 and 2.20 translated into average juvenile dispersal distances of 0.8, 1.4 and 2.2 km, respectively, reflecting values that are lower than, equal to or larger than known dispersal distances for adult massasaugas, respectively (Weatherhead & Prior 1992). For all simulations, individ- uals dispersed following a linear function and adults dispersed to a maximum of 2.00 resistance units, which translated into maximum dispersal of 2.5 km, and an average simulated dispersal distance of 1.4 km, reflecting the maximum and average range size of radio-tracked massasaugas (Weatherhead & Prior 1992). Mortality rates were set to reflect those published for massasaugas, where 65% of newly born snakes (Miller 2006) and 45% of adult snakes die (Harvey & Weatherhead 2006) every generation. The number of offspring produced by each mated pair followed a Poisson distribution with a k of 8, reflecting known litter sizes of wild massasaugas in Ontario (Parent & Weatherhead 2000). Landguth et al. (2010) conducted similar simulations, but ours differ in two important ways. First, Landguth et al. This is unrealistic for our study system as roads are rarely complete barriers to dispersal (Shepard et al. 2008; Holderegger & Di Giulio 2010). Landguth et al. (2010) explored lag time to detection of barriers across a range of adult dispersal thresholds from 10 to 60 km. Massasaugas have comparatively low dispersal (<2 km), and the current simulations vary juvenile dispersal thresholds and explore lag time to detection using simulation parameters that are realistic to our study species. To address our second major objective (potential confound between water and roads), we simulated gene flow across a 533 km2 subset of the raster layer used in the landscape resistance analysis south of Parry Sound. We chose this landscape because we found significant correlations between genetic distance and models of IBR that included both water and roads as barriers to gene flow. These simulations allowed us to reconstruct the inferred processes to test whether simulated data matched our empirical results. For the first 100 generations, individuals dispersed and mated across a landscape where water alone restricted gene flow (IBR01 model, Table 1). After 100 generations, roads were added onto the landscape (IBR03 model, Table 1) and simulations continued for a further 50 generations. Given a massasauga generation time of 2–6 years, this represents 200–600 years of mating prior to European settlement and 100–300 years postsettlement. We generated 2792 individuals to roughly represent a population density of 5 snakes/km2 distributed across pixels with a resistance value of 1. Both adults and juveniles dispersed following a linear function with a threshold value of 2.3 resistance units. This value is higher than the threshold for the first simulation because resistance units are not directly comparable to Euclidean geographic distance, but depend on the specific landscape context. However, preliminary runs showed that this translated into approximately 1.3–1.5 km average dispersal distances that match empirical averages reported for massasaugas (Weatherhead & Prior 1992) and also those used in the first simulation. All other simulation parameters were the same as our first simulation set. For all simulations, initial populations had 12 neutral loci each starting with 10 alleles. Loci followed a k-allele mutation model with a mutation rate of 0.0005 per locus per generation, which represents the average mutation rate for microsatellite markers across taxa and loci (Estoup & Angers 1998; Selkoe & Toonen 2006). CDPOP simulations are stochastic; thus, we ran 10 Monte Carlo replicate runs for each simulation, sampling genotypes every five generations, to ensure that we understand the average outcomes for each set of parameter values. The genotypes of each sampled generation were input into SPAGEDI to generate matrices of Rousset’s ar (Rousset 2000). For the first simulations, we performed partial Mantel tests between genetic and geographic distances, and genetic distances and the road-barrier model of IBR (IBRroad), controlling for IBD for each sampled generation (pre- and postroad introduction). This was repeated for each simulation using a subset of 100 randomly chosen individuals. For our second set of simulations, we performed three sets of partial Mantel tests to address separate hypotheses. First, water alone should be detected as a barrier to gene flow before the introduction of roads, and we tested this with Mantel tests between genetic distances and an IBR matrix representing water alone as a restrictor of gene flow (IBRwater), controlling for IBD. Second, an IBR model incorporating both water and roads together as restrictors (IBRwater + roads) should show significant correlations with genetic distance only after the introduction of roads onto the landscape, which we tested with Mantel tests between genetic distances and IBRwater + roads, controlling for IBD. Finally, any independent effects of roads should be detected only after their introduction onto the simulated landscape, and to test this, we performed partial Mantel tests on IBRroads controlling for IBRwater. We repeated this using a subset of 56 randomly chosen individuals across the landscape, to approximate the actual number of massasaugas sampled in our empirical analysis. We also apply a two-step causal modelling approach (Wasserman et al. 2010) in an attempt to further parse out the confounding effects of water and roads on genetic structure (Appendix S1, Supporting Information).

Microsatellites had an average of 10.3  3.6 alleles per locus for eastern Georgian Bay and 10.9  4.3 alleles per locus for the Bruce Peninsula (Table S1, Supporting Information). All loci were in HWE. Scu214 and Sca3D6 exhibited linkage disequilibrium in one locale in eastern Georgian Bay. Six pairs of loci showed evidence of linkage disequilibrium in a single locale on the Bruce Peninsula. Departures from linkage equilibrium within populations can lead to over- or underestimates of population structure by Bayesian assignment tests (Falush et al. 2003); however, Bayesian assignment appears to be robust to violations of this assumption when linkage is weak (Falush et al. 2003; Hauser et al. 2006). Because patterns of linkage between loci were neither pervasive nor consistent across locales, all loci were used in analyses. DIC values for the global assignment test reached a plateau at k = 3, and revealed three genetic clusters, one in the Bruce Peninsula and two in eastern Georgian Bay lying north and south of Parry Sound (Fig. S1, Supporting Information). For the analysis within eastern Georgian Bay, DIC values reached a plateau at k = 4, which we judged to be the ideal cluster number. These clusters show a clear geographic trend, splitting the north into two clusters and separating individuals sampled from the southern mainland from those of Beausoleil Island (Fig. 1). For the Bruce Peninsula, DIC values did not plateau, so we chose the ideal number of clusters based on barplots. No new clusters arose after k = 2, which we designated as the number of clusters for this region. Mapping the cluster assignment of individuals revealed a distinction between Lyal Island and the mainland, but no further population subdivision of mainland snakes (Fig. 1). Calculations of pairwise Fst revealed low but significant differentiation among diagnosed clusters (Table S5, Supporting Information).

Mantel tests between genetic and geographic (IBD) distance were not significant in the Bruce Peninsula (Mantel r = 0.028, P = 0.721), but were significant north of Parry Sound (Mantel r = 0.221, P = 0.001) and south of Parry Sound (Mantel r = 0.241, P = 0.001). On the Bruce Peninsula, none of the IBR models significantly correlated with genetic distance after factoring out IBD (Table 1). North of Parry Sound, three IBR models were significantly correlated with genetic distance after factoring out IBD; all three included water alone as a restrictor to gene flow. However, these models were not significant after sequential Bonferroni correction (Table 1). Applying a second round of causal modelling to the top-ranked model (IBR07) revealed that all three IBR models are equally supported (Table S6, Supporting Information). Fifteen models of IBR showed significant correlations with genetic distance after controlling LANDSCAPE GENETICS OF RATTLESNAKES 4489 for IBD south of Parry Sound; however, only five remained significant after sequential Bonferroni correction (Table 1). All five models included open water and roads as restrictors of gene flow, but not dense forest. When we subsampled south of Parry Sound using only 29 random individuals, no Mantel r-values were significant; however, the ranking of IBR models remained the same (Table S4, Supporting Information). The second round of causal modelling revealed that all five of these models and IBR17 are equally supported (Table S6, Supporting Information).

For our first simulations across a neutral landscape, significant IBD was apparent after only five generations in Mantel tests across all combinations of juvenile dispersal thresholds and population density (Fig. S2, Supporting Information). Following the imposition of a semipermeable road barrier, partial Mantel tests indicated significant correlations between IBRroad and genetic distance after five, and 10 generations for dispersal thresholds of 0.8, and 1.4 km, respectively, but were never significant for a juvenile dispersal threshold of 2.2 km, at both low (4 snakes/km2) and high (6 snakes/km2) population densities (Fig. 2a,b). All significant correlations between roads and genetic distance disappeared when we limited partial Mantel tests to 100 randomly chosen individuals (Fig. For the second simulation set across the landscape south of Parry Sound, partial Mantel tests between genetic distances and IBRwater were significant after only five generations (Fig. 3a). The same result was found for tests using IBRwater + roads (Fig. 3a). These two patterns remained relatively consistent when genotypes were subsampled using 56 randomly chosen individuals, with significance appearing after 10 generations (Fig. After the imposition of semi-permeable road barriers, significant independent effects of roads were not detected by partial Mantel tests between genetic distance and IBRroads, factoring out IBRwater, for either the full or subsampled data sets (Fig. Two-step causal modelling did not support IBRwater + roads as the top hypothesis of landscape resistance after roads were added to the simulated landscape (Fig. S3, Supporting Information). After imposition of roads onto the landscape, partial Mantel tests between genetic distance and IBRwater + roads factoring out IBRwater were nonsignificant while tests between genetic distance and IBRwater factoring out IBRwater + roads were (Fig. S3, Supporting Information). Empirical and simulated genetic distance matrices were significantly correlated both before and following simulated road introduction (Fig. S5, Supporting Information).

We find differences in the amount of genetic clustering between our replicate landscapes, but also local differences in the effect of each landscape on genetic structure of eastern massasaugas. Our simulations imply that genetic structure can arise quickly, but also that spatially correlated landscape features in landscape genetic models may confound interpretation. Our results considered together reveal open water as having the clearest impact on genetically structuring of this species, with a lesser, and correlated, signal from roads. Computer simulations enhanced our understanding of the contributions of spatially confounded landscape-level processes.

The distinction between snakes north and south of Parry Sound was strong, as evidenced by low admixture between these sites (Fig. 1). Two aspects of topography might explain this disjunction. First, massasaugas rarely stray more than 10 km from the shoreline near Parry Sound (Weller & Oldham 1992), and thus dispersal of snakes around the Parry Sound inlet is restricted to a narrow corridor. Second, the town of Parry Sound lies between the clusters and likely has formed an impermeable barrier for massasaugas at least over the last few decades (~70 years, 11–35 massasauga generations). Gene flow appears to be less restricted between NED and KB, and no obvious contemporary landscape features coincide with the boundary between the two. An alternative, but not mutually exclusive explanation for the genetic structure of eastern Georgian Bay is that it reflects past demographic or colonization history. Irwin (2002) showed that stochasticity of demographic processes could produce strong phylogeographic breaks even when barriers to gene flow are absent, when individuals are continuously distributed. Further, colonization (e.g. following glacial re-treat) can cause spatial clustering of allele frequencies (Ibrahim et al. 1996). Similarly, genetic drift acting on the leading edge of an expanding population can allow ‘surfing’ of low-frequency alleles into colonized ranges, resulting in differentiation between colonized vs. ancestral populations. (Excoffier & Ray 2008). Finally, Chiucchi & Gibbs (2010) suggested that fragmentation of massasauga populations likely pre-dated European settlement because patterns of historical and contemporary gene flow among isolated populations are similar. This does not preclude the possibility that specific features have contributed to genetic breaks over hundreds of generations nor to the possibility that anthropogenic habitat alteration might alter gene flow within clusters. Recent simulation studies have shown that assignment tests may falsely identify genetic clusters in the presence of IBD (Safner et al. 2011; Blair et al. 2012; Meirmans 2012). We detected significant IBD in eastern Georgian Bay, both south and north of Parry Sound (Table 1). This result was expected as massasaugas exhibit extremely limited dispersal (Weatherhead & Prior 1992), but also suggests the possibility that clustering in eastern Georgian Bay could be an artefact of this underlying pattern. Unlike other assignment programs, the TESS algorithm controls for spatial autocorrelation of allele frequencies, which should theoretically minimize such confounded inference (Durand et al. 2009; Meirmans 2012).

Both spatial assignment tests and landscape resistance analyses imply that water limits massasauga dispersal at multiple scales. Strong differentiation between the Bruce Peninsula and eastern Georgian Bay shows that long-distance dispersal across Georgian Bay is extremely rare if it occurs at all. This differentiation is not unanticipated as large bodies of water present a major barrier to dispersal for many terrestrial snake species (e.g. King & Lawson 2001; Row et al. 2010). The relationship between water and genetic structure holds true at smaller spatial scales; within regional populations, both Lyal and Beausoleil Islands are genetically differentiated from the mainland Bruce Peninsula and eastern Georgian Bay, respectively (Fig. 1), and within the cluster of snakes south of Parry Sound, we found a significant relationship between genetic distance and IBR models that included both water and roads as impediments to dispersal.

The most highly supported IBR model south of Parry Sound included both water and roads as restrictors of gene flow (Table 1). This was predicted as roads present major barriers to movement and significant sources of mortality for many animals including many snakes (e.g. Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis, Shine et al. 2004; Pantherophis spiloides, Row et al. 2007; Crotalus horridus, Clark et al. 2010). Roads influence genetic structure in animals through modification of behaviour and direct mortality (Holderegger & Di Giulio 2010), both likely contributing to the pattern of landscape resistance. For example, Shepard et al. (2008) found that massasaugas crossed roads in Illinois significantly less than expected. Similarly, Rouse et al. (2011) found that radio-tracked massasaugas never crossed an old highway south of Parry Sound, but readily crossed a newly constructed highway in the same region. This implies that massasaugas develop avoidance behaviour in response to roads over substantial time. Road mortality is probably a leading factor in decline of massasaugas across the species range as hundreds of massasaugas are killed on local roads annually (Parks Canada 2010). High road mortality can diminish local abundance and limit the number of individuals exchanged between populations on opposite sides of roads, diminishing gene flow, decreasing Ne and ultimately leading to population divergence. Contrary to predictions, dense forest did not appear to impede dispersal. Previous work showed that massasaugas use forest less than would be expected by its availability on the landscape (Harvey & Weatherhead 2006; Moore & Gillingham 2006; Rouse et al. 2011). However, these studies quantified habitat based on telemetry locations, whereas only dispersal events that lead to gene exchange are measured in studies such as ours. Although massasaugas might not use forested habitats often for foraging, thermoregulation or protection, these habitats may still be used for dispersal.

We found regional differences in the effect of landscape on gene flow. On the Bruce Peninsula, we found no spatial structuring suggesting panmixia. North of Parry Sound, spatial structure was best characterized as IBD, whereas south of Parry Sound structure reflected IBR. Most landscape genetic analyses tend to focus on a single landscape. Our work joins an increasing number of studies that reveal discordant patterns of spatial structure across distinct locales (Keyghobadi et al. 2005; Moore et al. 2011; Short Bull et al. 2011). (2011) suggested that barriers to gene flow are detectable only if they are relatively continuous (i.e. not patchily distributed) across the landscape. Therefore, the contrasting results from our analysis might simply reflect differences in the composition or configuration of landscape features in our sampling locales. Matching this prediction, water is more abundant and continuous south of Parry Sound compared with the north and on the Bruce Peninsula (Table S2, Supporting information). Thus, the failure to detect water as a barrier in both the Bruce Peninsula and north of Parry Sound might reflect a true lack of influence of the feature on gene flow in these two regions – where water is comparably rarer and less likely to limit movement (Moore et al. 2011; Short Bull et al. 2011). We did not account for variability in barrier strength of roads across the landscape (aside from separation of major and minor roads), and this likely decreased their observed relationship with genetic distance. The lack of IBD and spatial structure on the Bruce Peninsula is surprising given the apparently low vagility of this species and the potentially high mortality caused by roads. Consistent with the Bayesian clustering results, lack of structure potentially implies that massasaugas within the Bruce Peninsula are relatively insensitive to landscape barriers or that the effects of water and roads on gene flow are too weak to detect. Alternatively, regional variation in the effect of landscape might reflect divergent demographic histories on the Bruce Peninsula compared with eastern Georgian Bay. For example, Chiucchi & Gibbs (2010) found that the Bruce Peninsula population of massasaugas had the largest historical Ne, over twice the size estimated for 10 localities across the range including all sampled Ontario populations (Killbear, Beausoleil Island, Wainfleet Bog, Ojibway Prairie). Thus, populations on the Bruce would experience less drift, slower population divergence and slower emergence of IBD and other spatial structure compared with eastern Georgian Bay (Wright 1948; Nei et al. 1975). Using a sibship assignment method (Wang 2009), which should reflect a more contemporary estimate of population size, we found that Ne of the Bruce, south of Parry Sound and Killbear were equally small (Appendix S1, Fig. S4, Supporting Information). Together, this suggests that contemporary genetic population structure reflects a lasting signal of historical population size in the Bruce Peninsula. Finally, local differences might simply reflect disparities in sampling intensity. Indeed, when we subsampled 29 random individuals from south of Parry Sound to match sample size north of Parry Sound, all significant IBR effects disappeared (Table S4, Supporting Information). This implies that small sample size limits our ability to detect landscape genetic correlations. However, a recent simulation study showed that the accuracy of landscape genetic correlations is not strongly affected by sample size, but rather by the number and variability of loci (Landguth et al. 2012). North of Parry Sound, three models of IBR that included water as the sole restrictor of gene flow were marginally significant after removing the effects of IBD. Therefore, it is possible that more extensive sampling will reveal a significant effect of water on gene flow in future analyses.

Our simulations revealed important details about the evolution of spatial structure in relation to dispersal capacity, population size and landscape composition. First, IBR can develop extremely fast (5–10 generations) in response to a road barrier on an otherwise neutral landscape, when juvenile dispersal is limited, and population density is low (Fig. 2). Our results are consistent with Landguth et al. (2010) who found a lag time of 1– 15 generations for the detection of the genetic effects of linear barriers. However, they also found longer lag times when dispersal was ‘low’ (10 km threshold, 6–14 generations) compared with high (20–60 km, 1–5 generations) suggesting that our ability to detect the effects of contemporary barriers is limited for poor dispersers. In contrast, our results show that these effects can develop rapidly for species with extremely limited dispersal when populations are sufficiently small. Massasauga generation time is estimated to be between 2 and 6 years (Parks Canada 2010), suggesting that genetic consequences of roads built from the 1950s to the late 1990s can be detected in contemporary populations. This time frame is appropriate to the current study as most major highway development in both the Bruce Peninsula and eastern Georgian Bay took place from 1935–1950 (Bevers 2011) This alone does not confirm our empirical result that roads shape gene flow south of Parry Sound. Indeed, it is clear from our simulations that the presence of water can confound inferences of road effects on genetic structure (Fig. 3). Most strikingly, a model that included roads and water as apparent impediments to gene flow was significant long before roads were actually introduced onto the simulated landscape (Fig. This suggests that roads might not truly influence spatial genetic structure, but that the apparent significance of these elements was driven by spatially correlated water features. However, a comparison of the simulated and empirical causal modelling results suggests that our empirical detection of road effects south of Parry Sound could be real. Both steps of causal modelling on our empirical data indicated that water alone did not significantly influence gene flow across the landscape (IBR01, Table 1; Table S6, Supporting Information), whereas the influence of water alone was evident after just a short number of simulated generations (Fig. 3) and remained significant after the second step of causal modelling (Fig. S3, Supporting Information). It is possible that the true effect of water on massasauga dispersal is not constant across the landscape. For example, water bodies that are bordered by roads might pose larger barriers to dispersal as the presence of these two features likely coincides with increased shoreline development for human recreation.

Our study thus shows the dangers of including spatially correlated landscape features in landscape genetic models, an issue that is largely overlooked in the literature (Balkenhol & Waits 2009). Causal modelling is a powerful tool for selecting among highly correlated hypotheses of IBD, isolation by barrier and IBR (Cushman et al. 2006; Cushman & Landguth 2010); however, to our knowledge the utility of causal modelling approaches to select among alternative hypotheses of IBR has not been fully assessed. We show that apportioning out the effects of IBRwater from IBRroads successfully rejected roads as a driver of genetic structure before they were introduced onto the simulated landscape, but was not successful in detecting independent effects of roads after the road barrier was introduced (Fig. 3). Likewise, two-step causal modelling was unable to parse out the confounding effects of water and roads (Fig. S3, Supporting Information). Clearly, new statistical alternatives must be explored for selecting among correlated hypotheses of landscape resistance. This suggestion is especially relevant in the light of results from recent simulations that showed that partial Mantel tests are heavily biased when variables are autocorrelated (Guillot & Rousset 2013). However, we show that complementing landscape genetic analyses with computer simulations is extremely useful for validation of model choice (see also Gauffre et al. 2008; Researchers interested in detecting the genetic consequences of anthropogenic features can further avoid spurious inference through carefully articulated and replicated study designs (e.g. Marsh et al. 2008; Clark et al. 2010; Short Bull et al. 2011) and by verifying results from multiple independent data sources (e.g. Cushman & Lewis 2010). Our simulations also revealed the conditions under which spatial structure might not arise, and when landscape genetic analyses might fail to detect underlying landscape-level processes. For example, when 100 individuals were randomly drawn from our simulated data sets, partial Mantel tests failed to detect IBD when population density was high and juvenile dispersal was equal to or less than adult dispersal (Fig. S2, Supporting Information). This supports our assertion that the lack of spatial structure on the Bruce Peninsula could reflect a large Ne. Few studies have investigated the spatial ecology of neonate snakes, but most agree that juveniles disperse shorter distances than adults on average (Webb & Shine 1997; Cobb et al. 2005; Jellen & Kowalski 2007). However, studies also reveal considerable variation of juvenile dispersal distances among sampling years (Webb & Shine 1997), across populations of the same species (e.g. Jellen & Kowalski 2007), and within single litters (Cobb et al. 2005). Thus, regional differences in the contemporary population structure of massasaugas might be shaped both by variation in Ne and landscape composition, but also by different local tendencies for dispersal of juveniles. Interpretations of simulations depend on how well the parameters used reflect actual values for wild populations. The strength of landscape genetic relationships is strongly dependent on the composition and configuration of the landscape (Cushman et al. 2012). Our simulations were parameterized for a single species and a single landscape and might not be broadly applicable to other systems (Balkenhol & Landguth 2011). For example, water strongly outweighed roads in terms of landscape composition south of Parry Sound, which likely contributes to our inability to parse out the effects of the two. Finally, our simulations were simplified in two important ways. First, massasaugas have overlapping generations but our simulations did not reflect this. Overlapping generations effectively increase Ne; thus, we likely underestimate the lag time to detection of semi-permeable barriers to gene flow (Nunney 1993). Second, we assumed a constant population size through time. Future simulations could assess how the use of age-structured populations with overlapping generations might alter our results.

Our results suggest that landscape features differentially shape genetic structure of populations of massasaugas across the bulk of their range in Ontario. Open water restricts dispersal when it is highly abundant and continuous on a landscape. In contrast, roads do not consistently shape local populations of massasaugas. Rather, contemporary population structure more likely represents regional differences in population size and population history combined with landscape-level processes. Importantly, we show that the partial Mantel test, one of the most commonly used methods in landscape genetics and causal modelling are not sufficient to detect landscape effects on gene flow when features are spatially correlated and sample size is limited. Future analysis will further improve our knowledge of the environmental and demographic processes responsible for shaping massasauga populations. Although our study inferred the general effect of water and roads on populations, it is still unclear how these features specifically inhibit movement and the scale at which gene flow is impacted. At the level of inferred genetic clusters, future analyses should investigate the relative contribution of gene flow vs. drift across barriers to the emergence of genetic distinctions (e.g. Austin et al. 2004). Further, our simulations revealed that the high correlation between water features and roads on the landscape might have lead to spurious inference about the true effect of roads on contemporary populations. Our results thus suggest two possibilities: that roads have no effect on dispersal and the diagnosed effect is caused by preexisting water barriers; or, as we think, that roads accentuate the impermeability of existing barriers. To verify that roads do truly influence gene flow more detailed analyses with greater geographic sampling density should be undertaken that control for the co-occurrence of these two types of landscape elements. Finally, the contrasting patterns of population structure between the Bruce Peninsula and eastern Georgian Bay hint that distinct population histories have left a signature in contemporary populations. Testing between different models of historical range expansion, contraction and colonization using Approximate Bayesian’s computation (Beaumont et al. 2002) would give insight into the processes underlying the contemporary distribution of genetic clusters across the two regional populations (e.g. Row et al. 2011).
